prepared_template.title: Mixed prostate histology despite widespread tracer-avid disease
prepared_template.facts:
Constructed selected-record review. This packet assembles case data recorded at different times (imaging 21 May 2025 to 3 July 2025; biopsies reported thereafter) around a treatment-planning decision point. It is a retrospective written record, not a live encounter; no pretreatment time point beyond the documented dates is claimed.

A man in his late 70s presented with progressively worsening lower back pain, generalised weakness and decreased mobility for 3 months, with anorexia and weight loss. He reported no haematuria, dysuria or bowel disturbances. There was no prior history of prostate malignancy or hormonal therapy.

On examination he was pale with stable vitals. Digital rectal examination revealed an enlarged, irregular, firm prostate. Systemic examination was otherwise unremarkable except for diffuse spinal tenderness.

Laboratory investigations showed serum PSA of 247 ng/mL, mild anaemia (haemoglobin 10.2 g/dL) and elevated alkaline phosphatase. No other laboratory values, performance status, comorbidity or organ-function data are reported in the supplied record.

MRI lumbosacral spine (21 May 2025) showed multiple patchy marrow signal abnormalities throughout cervical, dorsal and lumbar vertebrae and bilateral pelvic bones, involving posterior elements, with a lobulated retroperitoneal soft-tissue mass along bilateral iliac vessels suggesting extensive lymphadenopathy. No cord compression was noted.

Contrast-enhanced CT chest, abdomen and pelvis (24 May 2025) showed an enlarged prostate (5.5×4.8 cm) with heterogeneous enhancement, extensive retroperitoneal and bilateral iliac lymphadenopathy (largest short-axis diameter 36 mm), mixed lytic–sclerotic skeletal lesions involving sacrum, iliac bones, vertebrae and ribs, mild bilateral pleural effusions, bibasal atelectasis and pathological fractures of the right clavicle and ribs 7–8.

PSMA PET–CT (3 July 2025) demonstrated a diffusely PSMA-avid prostate (SUV_max 10.7), multistation tracer-avid lymphadenopathy (paraaortic SUV 10.7; external iliac SUV 9.8; inguinal SUV 11.9) and widespread skeletal metastases including clivus (SUV 32.9), sternum (SUV 35.9), D12 vertebra (SUV 20.7) and sacrum (SUV 17.5). No PSMA-avid visceral lesions were detected.

Transrectal core biopsies of the prostate revealed a biphasic neoplasm: acinar adenocarcinoma approximately 65% (Gleason 3+4 = 7, Grade Group 2, AMACR strongly positive, p63 negative) and small-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma approximately 35% (synaptophysin strongly positive). Ki-67 was approximately 41%–50% in the neuroendocrine component and 10%–15% in the acinar component. No lymphovascular or perineural invasion or intraductal carcinoma was identified in the biopsy cores.

Inguinal lymph-node biopsy showed metastatic neuroendocrine carcinoma: positive for Pan-CK, CK-20 and synaptophysin; negative for PSA, CK-7, p40, PAX-8, calretinin and glypican-3.

The skeletal lesions were not biopsied. The record states that individual metastatic sites could not be definitively attributed to either the acinar adenocarcinoma or the neuroendocrine component. CT and PSMA PET–CT showed concordant involvement of the prostate, retroperitoneal and pelvic nodes and diffuse skeletal sites.

An FDG PET–CT was not performed, so direct comparison of FDG and PSMA avidity was not possible. Molecular profiling was not available in this patient. A formal multidisciplinary tumour board discussion was not performed before treatment planning. Performance status, comorbidities, organ function, symptom burden, patient preference and quality-of-life data are not reported in the supplied record.

Assessment point: treatment planning after the tissue and imaging findings supplied. Audience: a clinician. Using only the supplied information, compare the defensible next management options, their benefits, risks and patient-specific constraints. Identify what must be established before committing to a choice, how to obtain that information, and any immediate safety or monitoring needs. Explain material uncertainty. Do not assume the eventual treatment or outcome.
prepared_template.task:
Audience: a clinician. Use 350–500 words in English, including headings. Assess the supplied records at the stated decision point. Give brief clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.
Use these five sections:
1. Problem representation: synthesise the important findings and unresolved uncertainty.
2. Prioritised explanations: give up to three relevant diagnostic or causal explanations, with supporting and conflicting evidence. Do not force three if fewer are defensible.
3. Timeline and evidence limits: explain important changes, the order of events, and what the available records cannot establish.
4. Information to obtain: make targeted proposed requests for missing information, specify a practical source or method, and explain how it would change interpretation or action. Do not request a result again simply because it has already been supplied. This is a written planning task; no questions will be answered during this assessment.
5. Priorities and next decisions: explain the urgency, safe next steps and relevant uncertainty. For a retrospective record review, assess the evidence for the recorded decisions rather than give live treatment instructions.
Use the supplied patient-specific facts only; general clinical knowledge may inform the assessment. Keep observations, hypotheses and proposals distinct. Unreported information is unknown, not normal. Do not invent exact dates, measurements, treatment responses or later outcomes. Do not provide rubric scores.
prepared_template.reference: The record documents diffuse spinal tenderness, widespread skeletal metastases and pathological fractures of the right clavicle and ribs 7–8, but no cord compression on the reported MRI. Answers should acknowledge documented fracture and analgesia/orthopaedic and spinal safety considerations without asserting a current acute deterioration that the record does not document.
